meta.location: The land of Lehi-Nephi and the wilderness

world_behind.title: What three generations of this colony cost
world_behind.text: Zeniff bargained for land and got it on Lamanite terms. Noah taxed his own people a fifth part to build with. By the end of this chapter a foreign king takes half of everything and posts guards paid out of it. The rate the people carry more than doubles inside one chapter, and the guards are their own money.

world_behind.title: A wilderness that hides one group and catches another
world_behind.text: Alma's congregation walked into it in the previous chapter and the king's army could not find them. Noah's column flees into the same country here and is overtaken almost at once. The land is a refuge or a trap depending on who is moving through it, and the record lets the two outcomes sit a chapter apart without comment.

world_behind.title: Gideon arrives with no introduction
world_behind.text: He is described only as a strong man and an enemy to the king. He goes on to become one of the steadier figures in the record, and a city and a valley will later carry his name. The record gives him a sword before it gives him a role.

world_behind.title: How a king is removed here
world_behind.text: There is no trial, no council, and no succession law in sight. A private man draws a sword, an invasion interrupts him, the people burn the king themselves in the wilderness, and the kingdom is conferred on his son by popular act. Each step is reported without comment.

world_behind.title: The order to leave the women
world_behind.text: Verse 11 is a military decision: the men can outrun the Lamanites if they are not carrying anyone. Verse 12 records that many refused. Everything the colony has afterward comes from the ones who stayed.

world_behind.title: Two years of quiet, stated as such
world_behind.text: The chapter closes with continual peace for the space of two years. In this record that formula is usually a hinge, and the next chapter opens with Noah's priests watching Lamanite girls dance.

words.text: A split in a body of people, and it is the first thing that happens once the army comes home empty-handed. The verse gives the cause as reduced forces. The fracture follows from a failed manhunt.

Declared intent to do harm, spoken and not yet acted on. The lesser part breathes them out against the king. Luke uses the same construction of Saul before Damascus, and in both places the threatening comes first and something interrupts before it lands.

To refrain from killing when killing is within your power. Noah asks for it in the anguish of his soul, and the record grants that his motive was his own life rather than his people's. Gideon spares him anyway, which makes the mercy independent of the plea that requested it.

Held or captivated, in the older sense that carries a suggestion of enchantment rather than mere approval. The Lamanites are said to have compassion on the captives and to be charmed with the beauty of their women, with the two given as one reason. It occurs once in scripture.

Bestowed by someone who had it to give. The kingdom is conferred upon Limhi by the people, not inherited from his father, and the record picks a word that names the transfer as an act by the givers. His first use of the office is to swear tribute to a foreign king.

To trouble or harass, without the modern narrower sense. The chapter closes by saying the Lamanites did not molest them nor seek to destroy them for two years, a description of a garrison behaving itself.

phrases.term: Having searched in vain for the people of the Lord
phrases.text: The army sent to destroy Alma's congregation comes home having found nothing, and the record names the fugitives by what they now are rather than by who they were. The failed search is also what reduces the forces and starts the split in the next verse.

phrases.term: He fled and ran and got upon the tower which was near the temple
phrases.text: Three verbs of retreat in a row, and then a structure this record has described before. The king does not rally anyone, call for guards, or give an order. He runs, and the highest point in the city is the place he goes.

phrases.term: The king was not so much concerned about his people as he was about his own life
phrases.text: The abridger stating a motive outright instead of letting the scene carry it. Noah had just said the Lamanites would destroy my people. The sentence takes the plea apart and then reports that Gideon spared him regardless.

phrases.term: Had rather stay and perish with them
phrases.text: The refusal that saves the colony. Many would not leave, and the verse puts their reasoning as a preference. The rest left their wives and their children and fled, and the record gives that clause the same flat treatment.

The phrase used of Abinadi two chapters earlier, now used of the king who ordered it. Abinadi had said the life of king Noah would be valued as a garment in a hot furnace. The men who carry it out are the ones Noah told to abandon their families.

phrases.term: After they had ended the ceremony
phrases.text: Six words covering whatever was done between the burning and the return, and the record never says what it was. The phrase occurs once in scripture. Whatever the ceremony was, the men went back rejoicing and reported it to Gideon.

phrases.term: He did support his guards out of the tribute which he did receive
phrases.text: The occupation pays for itself. Guards are posted so the people cannot leave, and the wages come from the half they hand over. The arrangement is described without any comment at all, in the same voice as the two years of peace that follow it.

verses.label: v. 1–4
verses.title: A sword at home
verses.text: The manhunt fails, the forces shrink, the people split, and a man named Gideon draws on the king. Four verses take the kingdom from a search party to an assassination attempt, and nothing supernatural is involved in any of it.

verses.label: v. 5–8
verses.title: Up the tower, and a trade
verses.text: Noah runs, climbs, sees the Lamanites, and bargains for his life with the news. The record grants that the argument worked and then says what he actually cared about. Gideon's sword goes down for a reason that turns out to be true even though the man saying it was lying about why.

verses.label: v. 9–12
verses.title: The order to run
verses.text: The king leads the flight, the Lamanites overtake them, and the order comes to leave the wives and children. The verse that follows splits the men in two with no adjectives attached to either group.

verses.label: v. 13–15
verses.title: Daughters, and terms
verses.text: The families who stayed send their daughters out to plead. The Lamanites spare them, take them captive, and set the price: Noah handed over, half of everything, and tribute year by year. The colony's whole future is settled in one verse by people who were not consulted.

verses.label: v. 16–17
verses.title: A son who is not his father
verses.text: Limhi is introduced as one of the captives, wanting his father alive and under no illusions about him. The record calls him a just man in the same sentence that says he knew the iniquities, which makes the judgment and the loyalty coexist.

verses.label: v. 18–24
verses.title: What the men did to the king
verses.text: Gideon's scouts find the survivors; the survivors have sworn to go back and avenge or die; the king forbids it; they burn him. Then the priests run, and the men return rejoicing because the families they abandoned were not killed.

verses.label: v. 25–29
verses.title: A kingdom on a lease
verses.text: An oath from the Lamanite king, an oath from Limhi, half of everything, guards funded by the tribute, and two years of quiet. Limhi is said to establish the kingdom and establish peace, in a chapter where he controls neither.

chapter.title: The tower is used once, for the opposite of its purpose
chapter.text: It was built so a king could look out over land he did not own. Its one recorded use is as a refuge from one of his own subjects, and what he sees from the top is an army he cannot stop. It buys him four verses.

chapter.title: Abinadi's sentence on the king is executed by the king's own people
chapter.text: The prophecy valued Noah's life as a garment in a hot furnace. He dies by fire in the wilderness, and the men who do it are the ones he ordered to leave their wives behind.

chapter.title: The bondage prophecy lands in the same chapter
chapter.text: Delivered into the hands of their enemies, brought into bondage, none to deliver them except the Lord. Verse 15 fixes the rate at one half and verse 28 posts guards paid out of it. The record does not connect the two passages; it simply reports the terms.

chapter.title: The abridger names a motive out loud
chapter.text: Verse 8 is one of the few places where this record tells us what a man was privately thinking instead of showing it and moving on. It is used to convict a king who is about to be spared.

chapter.title: The colony survives on an act of disobedience
chapter.text: The order was to abandon dependents. The families that exist afterward are the ones whose men ignored it, and the plea that saves everybody comes from their daughters.

chapter.title: Limhi is handed the throne
chapter.text: He does not succeed by right; the people hand him the office after burning his father. His first sworn act with it is to promise half of everything to a foreign king, so what he receives and what he signs away arrive in the same verse.

chapter.title: Nobody in the chapter moralizes the outcome
chapter.text: No speech interprets the tribute as deserved, and no prophet appears. The record gives motives, numbers, an oath, a garrison, and two years of peace, and lets the previous six chapters do the explaining.

chapter.title: Role in the unit
chapter.text: Mosiah 9 and 10 are Zeniff's own record; 11 through 17 are Noah and Abinadi; 18 is Alma leaving; 19 through 22 are Limhi's bondage and escape. This chapter is where the throne changes hands and the record's attention moves from a prophet to a captive people.

applications.title: Watch what your monuments are actually for
applications.text: The tower was built to look impressive and to look down on neighbors. Its one use was as an escape route. Ask what the things you have built would actually be good for on a bad day.

applications.title: A true argument can still be a self-serving one
applications.text: Noah was right that the Lamanites were coming and wrong about why he was saying it. Being correct is not evidence of good faith, in others or in yourself.

applications.title: Notice who refuses the efficient order
applications.text: The instruction to leave the families was militarily sound and the people who ignored it are the reason there is anything left. Efficiency and survival are not always the same calculation.

applications.title: Loyalty and clear sight can coexist
applications.text: Limhi wanted his father spared and was not ignorant of his father's iniquities. You do not have to pretend about someone in order to want good for them.

applications.title: Check who is paying for your constraints
applications.text: The guards keeping the people in were funded by the people's own tribute. When something is limiting you, it is worth asking where its budget comes from.

applications.title: Treat two years of quiet as data
applications.text: The chapter ends on peace, and the peace is a garrison behaving itself. Before calling a calm period a resolution, check whether anything underneath it has changed.

applications.title: Give the office and the obligation the same weight
applications.text: Limhi received a kingdom and immediately swore away half its produce. When you take on authority, look at what comes attached before you count what you gained.

questions.text: What have I built mostly so that it could be seen?
When have I made a true argument for a reason I would not say out loud?
What order have I followed that I should have refused?
Whom do I love without illusions, and whom do I love by keeping them?
What have I stopped asking about because the account skips over it?
What am I calling peace that is really a well-behaved guard?
